newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW-S.African futures market braced for boom.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-S.African futures market braced for boom.

text.p: The South African Futures Exchange (Safex) is gearing up for a threefold increase in turnover by the end of next year as it launches a range of new products and cashes in on bond market reforms.

Safex posted a 38 percent increase in turnover to 278 billion rand ($62.4 billion) last year, an amount that could treble within the next 12 to 18 months, according to Stuart Rees, chief executive of the world's 26th largest futures exchange.
Earlier this week Safex announced it would begin trading rand/dollar currency futures on April 30 following Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's recent exchange control relaxations.

"With the introduction of the currency contract, the reduction in the bond settlement period and the possible introduction of equity options, we see our volumes increasing possibly threefold in the next year to 18 months," Rees said in an interview with Reuters.

Currency traders said initial restrictions on the rand contract, which for now will be traded only by authorised dealers and non-residents, would limit volumes in the short-term. Rees agreed, but said once exchange controls were relaxed further, interest would grow.
"The currency contract should, within a short period of time after the relaxation of exchange controls, be trading in the order of 10,000 or 20,000 a day," he said.

The new contract, which will be worth $100,000, faces competition from the recently launched Finex dollar/rand futures, which trades in Dublin and New York, and the launch of a similar Chicago Mercantile Exchange contract on May 7.
"There will be a degree of competition," he said.
An important factor in the launch of the local contract on April 30 was that it would complement the Reserve Bank's phased withdrawal from the forward currency market.
"Futures will allow them to reduce their role in the forward cover market and their reduction of that role will increase the liquidity of the currency contract," he said.

While the exchange had no immediate plans to launch any more currency-related products, Rees said the further relaxation of exchange controls would signal Safex's ability to enter the hard commodity futures market -- contracts on precious metals.
"It is not something that is at the forefront of our minds at the moment. Our concern is to get the currency contract and the interest rate contracts working," he said.
Turnover in its existing R150 and R153 bond futures is already showing signs of picking up ahead of the Bond Exchange's planned introduction of a three-day settlement period.
Rees said volumes in the two contracts had grown to around 100 million rand a day in recent months in anticipation of the reduction of the current 14-day bond market settlement period.
Further products towards the lower end of the yield curve were also in the pipeline, as was a wheat futures contract, on its agricultural division.

Safex had also re-entered talks with the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) about the on-again, off-again Equity Options Market (EOM), but Rees said these had to be seen in the context of talks about the possible integration of the two exchanges.

"In the light of those co-operative discussions, which are quite far advanced, the feeling was that Safex should perform the role of the derivatives exchange and the JSE the role of the spot market for equities."
A sticking point was eliminating the element of offsetting underlying spot positions against options positions.
"If we eliminated that element of the market...then we would be able to provide equity options within 30 to 60 days of being given the listing by the Registrar," Rees said.
-- Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003 ($ = 4.458 South African Rand)
